clue.text: Tremble when I get the doctor out

indicators.note: the doctor stands outside, so his letters go round the other two pieces

explanation.surface: Someone shakes nervously whenever they have to call out the GP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' puts DR on the outside of I and THE, splitting it D...R around ITHE.
explanation.definitionFit: To dither is to waver or quiver with indecision, a nervous trembling.

clue.text: Be economical in an awkward predicament

explanation.surface: Advice to save money when you are in a tight spot.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrape (by) is to live frugally; a scrape is also a tricky fix or jam one gets into.

clue.text: Room for expansion where there is heavy unemployment

explanation.surface: A description of a region with space to grow but few jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a development area was an official region of high joblessness given government aid to attract industry.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a zone set aside for building and growth; in UK policy, a designated jobless region receiving state help.

clue.text: Waterloo not as it might be

indicators.note: 'as it might be' suggests the letters could be arranged differently, signalling a reshuffle of the preceding words

explanation.surface: A remark that Waterloo is not as it might be, a complaint about the battle or the terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: Waterloo is a major London railway terminus; 'might be' rearranges NOT AS IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo is an example: one of London's main railway terminals.

clue.text: Sung novel?

parts.note: the words describe a seasonal song that is also the title of a Dickens book

explanation.surface: A question about a book that has been set to music.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's festive novella shares its title with the kind of song sung in December.

clue.text: Did a blue design on a flowering shrub

indicators.note: a design is a fresh arrangement, so the letters of the preceding words are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone painted a blue pattern on a garden bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Buddleia is a garden bush with long purple flower spikes, the butterfly bush.

clue.text: Bob finds a means of saving time

explanation.surface: A man called Bob discovers a quicker way to do things.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a short haircut, and a quicker route or method is also called this.

clue.text: Prudent boy goes back to the island, so it is said

indicators.note: the phrase signals that the letters built are only heard, then respelt

parts.words: boy goes back to the island
parts.note: the boy SID written backwards gives DIS, placed before CRETE, the Greek island

explanation.surface: A careful lad heads back to an island, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: SID backwards (indicated by 'goes back') is DIS; with CRETE it sounds like the answer when spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe careful, tactful behaviour that avoids giving offence.

clue.text: Out where tennis is played, so to speak

indicators.note: signals that the word is heard, not seen, so a different spelling goes in

parts.note: tennis is played on a court

explanation.surface: Someone describes where a tennis match is played.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket 'caught' is a way of being out; in non-rhotic British speech COURT and the answer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman dismissed by a catch is out; caught is one mode of dismissal in cricket.

clue.text: Timber growing or burnt

explanation.surface: A note that the wood is either alive or on fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A common hardwood tree yields this timber, and the powdery residue left after burning bears the same name.

clue.text: Least expensive variety of peaches by the tonne

indicators.note: a variety is a different arrangement, so the letters of the fruit word are mixed

explanation.surface: A fruit seller advertises a cheap kind of peach sold by the ton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' rearranges PEACHES into CHEAPES; T follows ('by').
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of cheap: lowest in price.

clue.text: Additional clauses that can be carried

explanation.surface: A legal remark about extra provisions that might be passed.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is an added clause to a bill or contract; riders are also people borne on horseback or vehicles.

clue.text: With which one can say what one likes?

definitions.text: With which one can say what one likes?

parts.words: With which one can say what one likes?
parts.note: the question describes the liberty to express any opinion

explanation.surface: A question about what lets a person speak their mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The civil right to express opinions without censorship or penalty.

clue.text: Before the queen takes note

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword convention for the queen

explanation.surface: The monarch takes note in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ere is an old-fashioned word for prior to.

clue.text: Quietly start again to take for granted

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical marking for quietly
to resume is to begin once more after a pause

explanation.surface: Advice to restart something softly.
explanation.definitionFit: To presume is to assume something is true without proof.

clue.text: He'd learn about how to manage again

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of the words are shuffled

explanation.surface: Someone will find out how to cope a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges HEDLEARN; the apostrophe in He'd gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To handle is to manage, so to handle something once more is to manage it again.

clue.text: Imitate a mule, it's frisky

indicators.note: frisky means lively and jumping about, so the letters of the words caper into a new order

explanation.surface: Copy a mule, which is in a playful mood.
explanation.definitionFit: To simulate is to mimic or copy the appearance of something.

clue.text: Admits father's to be laying on paint thickly

annotationWithheld.why: Admits father's to be laying on paint thickly: wordplay is presumably I'M + PA'S + TO, but no word in the clue gives I'M ('Admits' does not mean it) and 'be' is unaccounted for; no source found.
annotationWithheld.clue: Admits father's to be laying on paint thickly

clue.text: Take one's place presumably after having stood

explanation.surface: A note on sitting down once one has been standing.
explanation.definitionFit: To be seated is to occupy one's seat, and one naturally does so after standing up.

clue.text: Clergyman, one leaving church

indicators.note: leaving means going away, so the letter for one departs from the word

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A priest, one of many, departs from his church.
explanation.definitionFit: A minster is a large or important church, often a former monastery church, such as York Minster.

clue.text: Handy drawing

parts.note: handy hints at something done on a finger part, while meaning a quick small sketch

explanation.surface: A convenient picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief, rough outline or description, as small as could fit on a fingertip's nail.

clue.text: Ornament wealthy men who have been decapitated first

indicators.note: says the beheaded men come before the wealthy piece
decapitated means beheaded, so the first letter of the word men is lost

parts.note: taken as written before its head is cut off

explanation.surface: Decorate rich men who were beheaded earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who have been decapitated' removes M from MEN to leave EN, which 'first' puts before RICH.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrich is to adorn or embellish something, making it richer in appearance.

clue.text: Said to produce a smile?

parts.note: the words describe what a photographer asks subjects to say so their mouths form a grin

explanation.surface: A question about words that make people grin.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographers ask sitters to say this dairy word because it stretches the mouth into a grin.

clue.text: Gail, an eccentric from old England

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters of the name and the following word are scrambled

explanation.surface: Gail is an oddball from historic England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges GAILAN; the second 'an' is part of the fodder, not the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglia is the Latin name for England, used for the land of the Angles.

clue.text: A water colour?

parts.note: a water colour suggests a painting, but here means the hue of the ocean

explanation.surface: A question about a painting done in watercolour.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluish-green shade like the ocean's colour.

clue.text: Desert animal

explanation.surface: A creature of arid lands.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to betray or abandon one's side, and a rat is a rodent.

clue.text: Cowardly sort of spirit

parts.note: Cowardly points to the playwright Noel Coward, whose comedy title pairs this word with spirit

explanation.surface: A timid ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward wrote the comedy Blithe Spirit; 'Cowardly' means 'of Coward', not timid.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe means carefree and cheerful, the adjective in the title of Coward's ghost play.

clue.text: Spirited removal man

parts.note: suggests a lively furniture remover, but means someone who drives out spirits

explanation.surface: A lively removals worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who expels demons or ghosts from a place or person.
